content.title: Unit Conversions, Compound Units, and Dimensional Analysis
content.overview: This lesson focuses on how to accurately perform unit conversions on the SAT Math test, especially using dimensional analysis for compound units such as area, volume, and speed. Mastering these techniques effectively prevents errors caused by inconsistent units in complex calculations.
learning_objectives: Understand and apply conversion factors for single-unit conversions.
Master conversion rules for compound units, such as square and cubic units.
Use dimensional analysis to handle multi-step conversions and verify the reasonableness of results.

sections.title: Conversion Factors and Dimensional Analysis Basics
sections.content: The core of unit conversion is the "conversion factor," a fraction where the numerator and denominator are equal in value but have different units (e.g., 12 inches / 1 foot). Dimensional analysis is a method of ensuring the calculation path is correct by canceling units. During the calculation, treat units as algebraic variables: if the same unit appears in both the numerator and denominator, they can cancel each other out. The units remaining at the end must be the units requested by the problem.

sections.title: Compound Unit Traps: Area and Volume
sections.content: This is the most common trap on the SAT. When converting area (square units) or volume (cubic units), the conversion factor must also be squared or cubed accordingly. For example, if 1 yard = 3 feet, then 1 square yard equals $(3\text{ feet})^2 = 9\text{ square feet}$, not 3 square feet. Similarly, $1\text{ cubic yard} = (3\text{ feet})^3 = 27\text{ cubic feet}$.

sections.title: Multi-Step Conversion Process
sections.content:
When dealing with complex units (such as converting miles per hour to feet per second), establish a continuous multiplication chain. Use a conversion factor at each step to ensure old units are canceled and new units are introduced. For example: $(\text{miles}/\text{hour}) \times (\text{feet}/\text{mile}) \times (\text{hour}/\text{minute}) \times (\text{minute}/\text{second}) = \text{feet}/\text{second}$.

![Compound Unit Conversion Flow (mph to ft/s)](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/44e2316d-f1a8-4e25-9162-1abf0dd0be9c-1786502068114-443.webp)

worked_examples.question: The area of a rectangular garden is 54 square feet. Given that 1 yard = 3 feet, what is the area of the garden in square yards?
worked_examples.solution:
Step 1: Determine the conversion factor. 1 yard = 3 feet.
Step 2: Since this is an area conversion, square the conversion factor: $(1\text{ yard} / 3\text{ feet})^2 = 1\text{ sq yd} / 9\text{ sq ft}$.
Step 3: Calculate: $54\text{ sq ft} \times (1\text{ sq yd} / 9\text{ sq ft}) = 54 / 9 = 6\text{ sq yd}$.
The answer is 6 square yards.

worked_examples.question: A car travels at a speed of 88 feet per second. Given that 1 mile = 5280 feet and 60 minutes = 1 hour, what is the car's speed in miles per hour?
worked_examples.solution:
Step 1: List the initial speed: $88\text{ ft} / 1\text{ sec}$.
Step 2: Convert the distance unit: $(88\text{ ft} / 1\text{ sec}) \times (1\text{ mile} / 5280\text{ ft})$. The units are now miles/sec.
Step 3: Convert the time units: $(\text{miles}/\text{sec}) \times (60\text{ sec} / 1\text{ min}) \times (60\text{ min} / 1\text{ hr})$.
Step 4: Combine and calculate: $(88 \times 60 \times 60) / 5280 = 316800 / 5280 = 60\text{ miles/hr}$.
The answer is 60 miles per hour.

common_mistakes: Forgetting to square or cube the conversion factor when performing area or volume conversions.
Inverting the numerator and denominator of a conversion factor, causing units to accumulate rather than cancel (e.g., resulting in $\text{ft}^2/\text{yd}$ instead of yd).
Missing an intermediate step in a multi-step conversion (e.g., only converting hours to minutes but forgetting minutes to seconds).
exam_tips: Always write down the units: Write out the unit cancellation process on your scratch paper; do not just write numbers.
Check the dimensions: If the question asks for speed and your final unit is mile-seconds/foot, the conversion factor was placed upside down.
Use common sense to check: For example, when converting from a large unit to a small unit (like yards to feet), the numerical value should increase; otherwise, it should decrease.
content.recap: The key to unit conversion lies in constructing correct conversion factors and using dimensional analysis for unit cancellation. For square and cubic units, always remember to apply the corresponding power to the conversion ratio. By setting up equations formally, you can effectively avoid calculation errors.

knowledge_claims.content: A conversion factor is a fraction where the numerator and denominator are physically equal but have different units, making its numerical value equal to 1.
In dimensional analysis, units can be canceled between the numerator and denominator of fractions just like algebraic variables.
When performing area unit conversions, the conversion factor for the length units must be squared.
When performing volume unit conversions, the conversion factor for the length units must be cubed.
If 1 yard equals 3 feet, then 1 square yard equals 9 square feet; incorrectly believing it equals 3 square feet is a common trap.
Converting compound units (such as miles per hour) requires simultaneously handling units in both the numerator (distance) and the denominator (time).
If the units of the final calculation result do not match the units requested, the position of the conversion factor (numerator or denominator) may be inverted.
When converting a large unit (such as kilometers) to a small unit (such as meters), the numerical part typically increases.
Multi-step conversions should be achieved by multiplying multiple conversion factors in succession, ensuring each step cancels the old unit from the previous step.
In SAT problems, providing conditions like "1 foot = 12 inches" usually implies that dimensional analysis is needed to unify units.
